title: Gray Code
statement:
An **n-bit Gray code sequence** is an ordering of all `2^n` binary strings of length `n` such that any two consecutive strings differ in exactly one bit, and the last string also differs from the first in exactly one bit.

Many such sequences exist, so print one specific sequence, the **reflected Gray code** `G(n)`, defined recursively:

- `G(1)` is `0`, `1`.
- `G(k)` is every string of `G(k-1)` with a `0` placed in front, in the same order, followed by every string of `G(k-1)` with a `1` placed in front, in **reverse** order.

Given `n`, print `G(n)`.
inputFormat: A single line containing the integer `n`.
outputFormat: Print the `2^n` strings of `G(n)` on one line, separated by single spaces.

examples.explanation: Prefix `G(1)` with `0` to get `00 01`, then prefix the reversed `G(1)` (`1`, `0`) with `1` to get `11 10`. Consecutive strings differ in one bit, and `10` differs from `00` in one bit.
The first half is `G(2)` with a leading `0`; the second half is `G(2)` reversed (`10 11 01 00`) with a leading `1`.

hints: Write out G(1), G(2) and G(3) by hand and look at how each one is built from the previous one.
The second half of G(k) is the first half mirrored, with the new leading bit set to 1. Mirroring keeps neighbours one bit apart, and the middle pair differs only in the new leading bit.
Equivalently, the i-th string is the binary form of `i XOR (i >> 1)` padded to n bits, if you prefer to skip the recursion.
